subject: history
displayName: KS3 History — Sources, Evidence & Historical Enquiry
subtitle: How historians find, evaluate and use primary and secondary sources as evidence.

data.targetWord: anything from or about the past that historians can examine to learn about people, events or society

examples.en-GB: A medieval coin, a Tudor portrait and a Victorian census are all examples of historical sources.

data.targetWord: information taken from a source and used to support an answer to a specific historical question

examples.en-GB: A diary entry about long working hours becomes evidence when used to answer a question about child labour.

data.targetWord: a source created at the time being studied, or by someone directly connected to the event, such as a wartime diary or a medieval law

examples.en-GB: A soldier's letter written from the trenches in 1916 is a primary source for studying the First World War.

data.targetWord: a source created after the time being studied, often using primary sources to explain the past, such as a textbook or documentary

examples.en-GB: A history textbook chapter about the Norman Conquest written today is a secondary source.

data.targetWord: the background of a source: who made it, when and where it was made, why it was made, and who it was made for

examples.en-GB: The provenance of a First World War recruitment poster tells us it was created by the government to encourage men to join the army.

data.targetWord: what a source says, shows or contains, including its words, images, numbers, symbols and specific details

examples.en-GB: The content of the diary extract included descriptions of aching fingers and early morning starts before sunrise.

data.targetWord: the wider situation at the time a source was made, which helps explain why it was created and what its details mean

examples.en-GB: The context of a 1917 newspaper report about food shortages includes German submarine attacks on supply ships during the First World War.

data.targetWord: the reason a source was made, such as to record events, to persuade, to entertain, to inform, to criticise or to control behaviour

examples.en-GB: The purpose of a wartime recruitment poster was to persuade men to join the army.

data.targetWord: the people a source was created for, which can affect what the source includes or leaves out

examples.en-GB: A private diary has a very different audience from a public speech, which is why their contents may differ.

data.targetWord: a sensible idea worked out from the details of a source, going beyond simply copying what it says while remaining grounded in the evidence

examples.en-GB: From the detail that workers hid bread before soldiers arrived, we can make the inference that civilians feared food being taken from them.

data.targetWord: the process of checking one source against another to see whether they agree, disagree or add different details

examples.en-GB: Historians use corroboration by comparing a worker's diary with a factory inspector's report to check whether both describe similar conditions.

data.targetWord: how far a source can be trusted to give accurate information for a particular historical question

examples.en-GB: A wage record may be reliable for showing what workers were paid, but less reliable for capturing how workers felt about their conditions.

data.targetWord: how much a source helps answer a particular historical question, which is separate from whether it is completely reliable or unbiased

examples.en-GB: A propaganda poster is not reliable for showing the reality of battle but is very useful for studying how governments encouraged recruitment.

data.targetWord: a one-sided viewpoint in a source, which may come from the creator's beliefs, role, purpose, audience or limited knowledge

examples.en-GB: The factory owner's letter showed bias because it described workers as threatening rather than presenting a balanced account of the protest.

data.targetWord: something a source cannot tell us, or a reason it may give only a partial or one-sided view of the past

examples.en-GB: A limitation of the diary is that it only shows one apprentice's experience and may not represent all children in all factories.

data.targetWord: the viewpoint of a person or group, shaped by their experiences, beliefs and position in society

examples.en-GB: The factory owner and the factory worker had very different perspectives on the 1842 protest outside the gates.

data.targetWord: a focused historical question that guides investigation, such as 'How useful are town records for understanding medieval trade?'

examples.en-GB: A good enquiry question is specific and answerable using evidence, such as 'How far did factory life change children's work in industrial Britain?'

data.targetWord: a historical source in text form, such as a diary, letter, law, newspaper, court record, speech or book

examples.en-GB: The apprentice's diary is a written source that can be used as evidence about child labour in industrial Britain.

data.targetWord: a historical source in image form, such as a painting, poster, photograph, map or cartoon, which can show attitudes, technology, status and symbols

examples.en-GB: A First World War recruitment poster is a visual source that reveals how the government presented army service to the public.

data.targetWord: a historical source in spoken form, such as a recorded interview, memory, speech or song, often useful for groups whose experiences were rarely written down

examples.en-GB: Oral history interviews with people who moved to Britain in the 1950s are valuable sources for studying post-war migration.

data.targetWord: physical remains from the past, such as buildings, tools, pottery, coins, bones or burial sites, especially important for periods where written records are limited

examples.en-GB: Pottery found at a Roman villa is an archaeological source that can suggest wealth, trade links and daily life.

data.targetWord: a historical source using numbers, such as census records, wages, death rates, prices or trade figures, useful for showing patterns and changes over time

examples.en-GB: Census data from 1801 to 1891 is a statistical source that shows how rapidly industrial towns grew in population.

data.targetWord: a survey of land, people and wealth in England ordered by William I in 1086; useful for studying Norman control but limited because it reflects royal government concerns rather than everyday life

examples.en-GB: The Domesday Book is a useful primary source for studying land ownership in Norman England, though it was made for taxation purposes.

data.targetWord: information, often from a government or authority, designed to influence people's beliefs or actions, typically presenting a one-sided view

examples.en-GB: Wartime recruitment posters are examples of propaganda because they present army service positively to encourage people to join.

data.targetWord: an explanation or view of the past, usually constructed after the event by historians, teachers, museums or filmmakers, using available sources

examples.en-GB: A museum display about the Industrial Revolution is an interpretation because curators have chosen what to include and how to explain it.

data.targetWord: a place where written and digital records are preserved and made accessible for historians and researchers to study

examples.en-GB: Historians visit archives to access original documents such as court records, letters and government papers.

data.sentence: A source becomes ____ when it is used to answer a specific historical question.
A source created at the time being studied is called a ____ source.
The background of a source — who made it, when, where, why and for whom — is called its ____.
The wider situation at the time a source was made is called its ____.
Checking one source against another to see whether they agree is called ____.
A one-sided viewpoint in a source is called ____.
A sensible idea worked out from the details of a source, going beyond simply copying what it says, is called an ____.
A biased source may be less ____ for establishing facts but still very useful for studying attitudes and propaganda.
A Roman coin, a medieval tool and a Victorian building are all examples of ____ sources.
Census records, wage tables and death rates are all examples of ____ sources.
A focused historical question that guides an investigation is called an ____ question.
The reason a source was made — whether to persuade, record, entertain or warn — is called its ____.
Recorded interviews, spoken memories and community songs are examples of ____ sources.
A school textbook written today about the Roman Empire is an example of a ____ source.
The people a source was created for — its intended readers or viewers — are called its ____.
Something a source cannot tell us, or a reason it gives only a partial view, is called a ____.
Information created to influence people's beliefs or actions, typically from a government, is called ____.
How far a source helps answer a particular question — separate from whether it is fully accurate — is called its ____.

data.title: Steps of a historical enquiry in the correct order
items: Study the provenance, content and context of each source
Corroborate sources by checking them against each other
Build an evidence-based answer and judgement

data.title: Steps for writing a strong source usefulness paragraph
items: State what the source says or shows (content)
Consider who made the source and why (provenance)
Explain what the source cannot tell us (limitation)
Make a final judgement about usefulness

data.title: Steps for comparing two sources that disagree
items: Identify what each source says about the event
Note where the sources agree and where they differ
Consider the provenance of each source (who made it and why)
Explain why the difference might exist using context
Decide which source is more useful for the question and explain why
